extracted.intended_audience: war correspondents, newsroom editors, and general newspaper readers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and implicit operational rules for reporting from a combat zone where telephone/communications are severely constrained; focuses on filing copy with military signal officers, telephone priority, and transmission strategies (short bulletins vs. long dispatches).

rubrics_metrics.name: Military voluntary cooperation for security
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no censorship, but there is a code of voluntary cooperation for military security (which various correspondents interpret in various ways).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters are expected to follow a voluntary security code when reporting from the front; interpret this code conservatively to avoid compromising military operations. The page notes that correspondents vary in how strictly they apply this code.

rubrics_metrics.name: File copy with Signal Corps officer (queued transmission)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every correspondent must file with a signal corps officer what he wishes to telephone. The officer puts a number on it in the order received. The correspondent must wait until all copy ahead of his is cleared before he gets a crack at the telephone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submit intended copy to the signal corps officer for numbering/queuing. Expect to be placed in a strict first-come/first-served transmission queue and to wait your turn; plan reporting and timing accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telephone priority ordering (press third)
rubrics_metrics.description: The press comes third in priority on the telephone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that military and U.N. calls have higher priority; press transmissions can be interrupted or preempted by Army or U.N. priority calls. Do not assume continuous access to lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telephone time limits and transmission trade-off
rubrics_metrics.description: At first were limited to four minutes each, then to three but now it has been agreed to let each man take as long as he needs. The catch: the man who writes a lengthy story finds that the others who wrote short bulletins have gotten in ahead of him; his story may be better and more detailed, but it is likely to be so far behind as to be almost worthless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance completeness against timeliness. When lines are constrained, shorter bulletins are more likely to get through earlier; long, detailed dispatches risk arriving too late to be useful. Choose format based on urgency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compose and transmit in short segments (sentence-by-sentence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practically everyone writes a sentence or two at a time. He reads that one bit to his Tokyo office, then has to give up the telephone until his next turn (which may be hours).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a serial, modular writing approach: prepare short, self-contained sentences or paragraphs that can be sent as slots open. This maximizes chance of timely delivery under severe line constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt format to distribution needs (bulletins vs full features)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some special and syndicate writers, with less need for speed, write their stories all in one piece.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide before filing whether the piece should prioritize speed (short bulletins sent in segments) or depth (full-length feature written in one go). Syndicate or feature copy can be produced in full when timeliness is less critical; frontline dispatches should favor brevity.
